### ABB Context

- **Parent Composite ABB**: [GUID-SEC-AI-ABB-1.9.01 — AI Security Reference Architecture](GUID-SEC-AI-ABB-1.9.01.md)
- **Domain**: Domain 7 — AI Gateway Security
- **Capability**: Establishes the AI Gateway as a dedicated security enforcement plane positioned between consuming applications and AI model endpoints. The AI Gateway provides capabilities that are architecturally distinct from and complementary to the enterprise API gateway: prompt and response routing policy, guardrail and content safety policy enforcement, multi-dimensional token- and cost-aware rate limiting, DLP inspection at the AI data plane, external AI provider governance, and AI-specific audit evidence generation. This ABB defines *what* an AI Gateway security component must be and do, independent of the specific platform or product used to realize it.

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-2.9.07.md#abb-scope]

### ABB Scope

**In scope for this ABB:**

- Definition of the AI Gateway as a **distinct logical component** in the AI security reference architecture — separate from and complementary to the enterprise API gateway ([GUID-SEC-NETWORK-API-GW-2.2.04](../Network/GUID-SEC-NETWORK-API-GW-2.2.04.md))
- **Prompt and response routing policy** — directing inference requests to appropriate internal or external model endpoints based on content classification, data sensitivity tier, capability requirements, and BAA coverage status
- **Guardrail and content safety enforcement** at the AI data plane — evaluating and blocking policy-violating prompts before they reach model endpoints, and policy-violating responses before they reach consuming applications
- **Token-aware and cost-aware rate limiting** — multi-dimensional controls across request rate, token consumption per session, and estimated compute cost per identity and per period; additive to and non-overlapping with network-layer rate limiting at the enterprise API gateway
- **DLP inspection at the AI gateway tier** — detecting and blocking PHI, PII, and sensitive data in prompts and responses at a centralized enforcement point before data crosses security or provider boundaries
- **External AI provider governance** — acting as the single governed proxy for all outbound requests to third-party AI APIs (Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, OpenAI API, and equivalents), enforcing BAA routing rules and DLP policy before data leaves the enterprise network
- **AI-specific audit evidence generation** — capturing token counts, model identifiers, routing decisions, guardrail policy outcomes, DLP disposition, and session metadata to satisfy HIPAA audit control requirements and support security operations monitoring
- **Logical placement** of the AI Gateway within cloud service platform network topologies (AWS and Azure), including relationship to VPC/VNet segmentation, PrivateLink/Private Endpoints, and AI traffic flow
- **Scope boundary definition** between AI Gateway controls and enterprise API gateway controls, with explicit handoff points and non-overlapping responsibilities

**Out of scope for this ABB:**

- Enterprise API gateway security controls (authentication, WAF, standard HTTP-layer rate limiting) — governed by [GUID-SEC-NETWORK-API-GW-2.2.04](../Network/GUID-SEC-NETWORK-API-GW-2.2.04.md)
- AI model serving and inference infrastructure security — governed by [GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-2.9.03](GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-2.9.03.md)
- Application-layer prompt injection defense and output validation within consuming applications — governed by [GUID-SEC-AI-APP-2.9.04](GUID-SEC-AI-APP-2.9.04.md)
- AI governance, risk classification, and compliance program requirements — governed by [GUID-SEC-AI-GOV-2.9.06](GUID-SEC-AI-GOV-2.9.06.MD)
- AI observability, incident response procedures, and SIEM correlation rules — governed by [GUID-SEC-AI-OPS-2.9.05](GUID-SEC-AI-OPS-2.9.05.MD)
- Product or vendor selection for AI gateway platforms — addressed in the paired Reference Architecture Detail ([GUID-SEC-AI-GW-RAD-3.9.07](ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-RAD-3.9.07.md)) and subsequent Solution Building Blocks
- **Agentic AI and multi-turn orchestration** — guardrail and DLP enforcement for multi-step tool-calling chains, RAG pipelines, and agent-to-agent traffic where context accumulates across multiple turns, or where AI Gateway upstream traffic does not originate from a human-facing application; these patterns require controls not fully addressed by single-request guardrail and DLP evaluation and are explicitly deferred to a follow-on ABB or to the paired RAD (GUID-SEC-AI-GW-RAD-3.9.07) pending determination of the appropriate ABB-level treatment. **Technology economics note**: the 7-stage enforcement pipeline defined in this ABB adds per-request overhead; in an agentic workflow with 20–50 tool calls per session, this overhead compounds multiplicatively per turn. The follow-on agentic ABB will need to address session-level or batched enforcement rather than per-request enforcement to avoid making agentic AI operationally impractical at scale. Platform teams designing agentic solutions SHALL NOT assume this ABB's enforcement model is directly applicable to multi-turn agentic workloads without a performance impact assessment.

### AI Gateway vs. Enterprise API Gateway: Scope Boundary

The AI Gateway and the enterprise API gateway are complementary, non-redundant components. The enterprise API gateway performs authentication, WAF inspection, and standard controls **before** traffic is forwarded to the AI Gateway. The AI Gateway applies AI-specific enforcement **after** that handoff. Neither component substitutes for the other.

| Control | Enterprise API Gateway | AI Gateway |
|---|---|---|
| TLS termination and mutual TLS | ✓ Owns | — |
| Bearer token authentication (JWT / OAuth 2.0) | ✓ Owns | — |
| WAF — OWASP API threat protection | ✓ Owns | — |
| Standard request-rate limiting (requests/min per identity) | ✓ Owns | — |
| DDoS protection | ✓ Owns | — |
| AI prompt content policy and guardrail evaluation | — | ✓ Owns |
| Jailbreak and harmful content detection | — | ✓ Owns |
| Token-aware rate limiting (tokens/session, cost/period) | — | ✓ Owns |
| Model routing and abstraction | — | ✓ Owns |
| DLP inspection on AI prompts and responses | — | ✓ Owns |
| BAA-governed routing to external AI providers | — | ✓ Owns |
| AI interaction audit logging (token counts, model ID, guardrail outcomes) | — | ✓ Owns |

## Logical Interfaces

The following technology-agnostic interfaces define how this component ABB integrates with sibling ABBs, enterprise platforms, and external services. Vendor-specific implementation details belong in the corresponding SBB.

| Interface Name | Direction | Connects To | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| Consumer Request Intake | Inbound | APP -> GW | Authenticated inference requests from consuming applications, forwarded after enterprise API gateway authentication and WAF inspection |
| Enterprise API Gateway Handoff | Inbound | EntAPI-GW -> GW | Validated bearer tokens and standard security headers forwarded by the enterprise API gateway; the AI Gateway receives pre-authenticated traffic and applies AI-specific policy |
| Service Identity Request Intake | Inbound | SVC -> GW | Authenticated inference requests from backend services, batch processors, and event-driven pipelines operating under machine identities (service accounts, managed identities); these callers may not pass through the enterprise API gateway. Machine-origin callers SHALL authenticate to the AI Gateway using **RFC 8705 mutual-TLS (certificate-bound access tokens)**, with SPIFFE/SPIRE SVIDs as the required workload identity mechanism in containerised environments, per [GUID-SEC-IAM-NON-HUMAN-AND-AI-STRATEGY-2.2.12](../Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-NON-HUMAN-AND-AI-STRATEGY-2.2.12.md). Short-lived OAuth 2.0 client credentials with RFC 9449 DPoP are permitted as a compensating mechanism where mTLS is not achievable in a given deployment context; the SBB SHALL document the justification. The AI Gateway SHALL apply the same 7-stage enforcement pipeline to machine-origin traffic as to human-origin application traffic. |
| Model Routing Dispatch | Outbound | GW -> MODEL/INFRA | Policy-validated, guardrail-screened inference requests routed to designated internal model serving endpoints |
| External AI Provider Proxy | Outbound | GW -> External AI Svcs | BAA-governed, DLP-inspected requests to third-party AI APIs (Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, OpenAI); blocked and logged if a DLP policy violation or BAA routing constraint is not satisfied |
| Consumer Response Delivery | Outbound | GW -> APP | Guardrail-evaluated, DLP-screened model responses returned to consuming applications after full policy enforcement |
| Guardrail and Policy Feed | Inbound | GOV -> GW | Content safety policies, DLP rule sets, model allowlists, PHI routing restrictions, and rate-limit thresholds published by the AI Governance function |
| AI Gateway Security Telemetry | Outbound | GW -> OPS | Token usage metrics, guardrail violation events, routing decisions, DLP alert records, cost-limit triggers, and session audit records forwarded to enterprise SIEM |

### Assumptions

The following are treated as true in this ABB. If any assumption is invalid in a specific deployment context, the SBB must explicitly address the deviation.

| # | Assumption | Implication If False |
|---|---|---|
| A1 | The enterprise API gateway ([GUID-SEC-NETWORK-API-GW-2.2.04](../Network/GUID-SEC-NETWORK-API-GW-2.2.04.md)) authenticates and WAF-inspects all **human-origin** inbound AI inference traffic before forwarding to the AI Gateway. Machine-origin service callers (batch processors, backend services, event-driven pipelines) are governed by the `Service Identity Request Intake` interface and authenticate directly using RFC 8705 mTLS per [GUID-SEC-IAM-NON-HUMAN-AND-AI-STRATEGY-2.2.12](../Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-NON-HUMAN-AND-AI-STRATEGY-2.2.12.md) | The AI Gateway enforcement model assumes pre-authenticated traffic on all interfaces; unauthenticated traffic — from any origin — undermines identity-scoped rate limiting and audit record attribution |
| A2 | Network topology technically prevents direct application-to-model routing; consuming applications have no network path to model serving endpoints or external AI provider APIs that bypasses the AI Gateway | The mandatory enforcement plane (Principle 1) is a logical construct that depends on network-layer enforcement; without it the AI Gateway can be circumvented |
| A3 | The GOV function ([GUID-SEC-AI-GOV-2.9.06](GUID-SEC-AI-GOV-2.9.06.MD)) is operationally capable of maintaining all policy feed components this ABB depends on: data sensitivity tier registry, guardrail rule set, DLP rule set, BAA allowlist, and capability class registry | Without an operational GOV policy feed, the AI Gateway cannot enforce data sensitivity–based routing or maintain current enforcement policies; PHI-bearing use cases SHALL NOT deploy until GOV capability is confirmed operational |
| A4 | External AI providers requiring BAA coverage have executed BAAs with the organization before being added to the routing allowlist | The BAA routing enforcement capability (Principle 4) enforces allowlist membership; it cannot substitute for a missing executed BAA |
| A5 | Cloud platform Private Endpoint / PrivateLink capabilities are available and funded in all deployment regions | External AI provider private connectivity (Principles 4, 5) depends on private endpoint availability; deployments in regions without this capability require compensating controls documented in the SBB |

## Information Architecture

This section describes the data entities the AI Gateway owns, holds at rest, and generates as a security enforcement component. This is distinct from the enterprise AI data classification scheme defined in [GUID-SEC-AI-DATA-2.9.01](GUID-SEC-AI-DATA-2.9.01.md).

### Data Held at Rest

| Data Entity | Classification | Storage Location | Lifecycle |
|---|---|---|---|
| Guardrail policy rule set | Internal — GOV-provisioned | Local policy cache | Refreshed per GOV feed poll interval; prior version retained for rollback |
| DLP rule set | Internal — GOV-provisioned | Local policy cache | Refreshed per GOV feed poll interval |
| BAA-governed provider allowlist | Internal — GOV-provisioned | Local policy cache | Refreshed per GOV feed poll interval |
| Data sensitivity tier registry | Internal — GOV-provisioned | Local policy cache | Refreshed per GOV feed poll interval |
| Capability class registry | Internal — GOV-provisioned | Local policy cache | Refreshed per GOV feed poll interval |
| Rate-limit state counters | Operational — per-identity token and cost consumption; no prompt or response content | In-memory or distributed state store (identity-scoped) | Session or period window; not persisted beyond configured window |
| Local audit record buffer | Security — content hashes and context identifiers only; no full prompt or response content | Local durable buffer (pre-forward) | Retained until SIEM forwarding confirmed; then purged |

All cached policy data is read-only within the AI Gateway and is provisioned exclusively by the GOV function. The AI Gateway SHALL NOT modify or extend GOV-provisioned policy artifacts.

### Data Flows Mediated

The AI Gateway inspects and routes the following data flows. It does not persistently retain prompt or response content.

| Data Flow | Classification | Direction | AI Gateway Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| Inbound prompt — non-PHI | PII or Non-sensitive | APP → GW → MODEL | DLP inspect; guardrail evaluate; route per capability class; write audit hash |
| Inbound prompt — PHI | PHI | APP → GW → BAA-covered endpoint only | DLP inspect; guardrail evaluate; BAA verify; route; write HIPAA-compliant audit record |
| Model response — non-PHI | PII or Non-sensitive | MODEL → GW → APP | Guardrail evaluate; DLP inspect; deliver; write audit record |
| Model response — PHI | PHI | MODEL → GW → APP (BAA-governed context only) | Guardrail evaluate; DLP inspect; deliver; write HIPAA-compliant audit record |

### Core Principles

The following principles establish the normative foundation for the AI Gateway as a dedicated security enforcement component within Gainwell's AI security reference architecture. These principles address the AI data plane specifically and are complementary to — not replacements for — the application-layer security principles in [GUID-SEC-AI-APP-2.9.04](GUID-SEC-AI-APP-2.9.04.md) and the enterprise API gateway controls in [GUID-SEC-NETWORK-API-GW-2.2.04](../Network/GUID-SEC-NETWORK-API-GW-2.2.04.md).
page_texts.19:
[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-2.9.07.md#principle-1-ai-gateway-as-distinct-enforcement-plane]

#### Principle 1: AI Gateway as Distinct Enforcement Plane

**Description**: The AI Gateway functions as a dedicated security enforcement layer positioned between enterprise API gateway infrastructure and AI model endpoints. It is architecturally and operationally distinct from the enterprise API gateway and from individual model-serving components, and must be deployed as such in all production AI service topologies.

**Rationale**: AI workloads create enforcement requirements that general-purpose API gateways are not designed to satisfy — prompt content evaluation, token-aware cost control, model routing by data sensitivity, BAA-governed provider selection, and AI-specific audit evidence generation. Without a dedicated enforcement plane, these controls are either unimplemented or applied inconsistently at the application layer. A distinct AI Gateway ensures enforcement is consistent, auditable, and independent of individual application implementations.

**Capability Characteristics**:

- The AI Gateway SHALL be deployed as a distinct logical component — not co-located with or substituted by the enterprise API gateway — in all service topologies where AI inference traffic is present
- The AI Gateway SHALL be the single mandatory enforcement point for all AI inference traffic originating from enterprise applications; no application or service SHALL route inference requests directly to internal model serving endpoints or external AI provider APIs without passing through the AI Gateway
- The AI Gateway SHOULD be deployed in a dedicated network segment or zone, separated from enterprise API gateway infrastructure and from model serving infrastructure, to support independent policy management, scaling, and incident response
- The AI Gateway SHALL maintain its own policy configuration, audit log stream, and operational monitoring channel, independent of the enterprise API gateway configuration
- The AI Gateway SHOULD be realized using a platform capability that supports programmatic policy management (policy-as-code), enabling consistent, version-controlled policy deployment across cloud service platform environments
- The AI Gateway SHALL fail closed on unavailability: when the AI Gateway is degraded or unreachable, inference requests SHALL be rejected with a service-unavailable response and SHALL NOT be routed directly to model serving endpoints or external AI provider APIs as a bypass path; under no failure condition SHALL AI inference traffic reach model endpoints without traversing AI Gateway enforcement
- Because the AI Gateway is a mandatory single enforcement point, its availability directly determines the availability ceiling of every AI capability in the enterprise; the AI Gateway SHOULD be deployed in a high-availability configuration (active-active or active-passive with automatic failover) appropriate to the availability requirements of the AI use cases it serves; the availability target and HA topology SHALL be defined at the SBB level and SHALL be reviewed before the AI Gateway is placed on any clinical decision support or member-facing critical path
- Partial enforcement pipeline degradation — where the AI Gateway container is healthy but an enforcement stage (DLP inspection service, guardrail evaluation service, or policy cache) is unavailable or returning errors — SHALL be treated as a fail-closed condition for that stage: requests SHALL NOT be forwarded without the full enforcement pipeline completing successfully; the AI Gateway SHOULD support a configurable degraded-mode routing policy that restricts traffic to a defined set of low-risk capability classes when an enforcement stage is partially degraded, in preference to total service rejection, where the risk profile of those capability classes permits it
- **Enforcement pipeline latency budget**: Because the AI Gateway adds in-band overhead on every inference request, an enforcement pipeline latency budget SHALL be defined at the SBB level based on the latency requirements of the AI use cases served. The following guidance applies at this ABB level: (a) interactive applications (chat, real-time summarization, practitioner-facing tools) SHALL target a maximum enforcement pipeline overhead of 200ms end-to-end across all seven enforcement stages; implementations that cannot achieve this threshold with an LLM-based safety evaluator SHALL use a fine-tuned safety classifier; (b) non-interactive and batch applications MAY accept higher enforcement overhead consistent with their documented latency SLA; (c) the `enforcement_pipeline_latency_ms` field in the audit record SHALL be monitored continuously and SHALL trigger an operational alert when the 95th percentile exceeds the configured SLA threshold; (d) SBB selection of guardrail evaluation tooling SHALL include a measured latency profile under representative load, not only a capability assessment

**Reference**: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-7 (Boundary Protection); SC-7(13) (Isolation of Security Tools); SA-17 (Developer Security and Privacy Architecture and Design); CP-7 (Alternate Processing Site); CP-10 (System Recovery and Reconstitution); NIST AI RMF "Secure and Resilient" characteristic

#### Principle 2: Guardrail and Content Policy Enforcement at the Data Plane

**Description**: The AI Gateway SHALL evaluate all prompts and responses against a centralized content policy and guardrail rule set before traffic crosses AI data plane boundaries. Prompts that violate policy SHALL be blocked before reaching model endpoints; responses that violate policy SHALL be blocked before reaching consuming applications.

**Rationale**: Content safety controls implemented within individual applications are fragmented, application-specific, and bypass-prone. Centralizing guardrail enforcement in the AI Gateway ensures that every inference path — regardless of consuming application or model endpoint — is subject to the same policy baseline, that violations are uniformly blocked, and that guardrail decisions are auditable at a single enforcement point. Healthcare AI deployments face particular risk: a prompt or response bypassing application-layer controls can expose PHI, produce clinically dangerous content, or generate outputs that violate HIPAA Privacy Rule minimization requirements.

**Capability Characteristics**:

- The AI Gateway SHALL apply guardrail policy evaluation to all inbound prompts before forwarding to any model endpoint; prompts that match jailbreak, harmful content, or data-exfiltration policy rules SHALL be blocked and logged with a policy outcome record
- The AI Gateway SHALL apply guardrail policy evaluation to all outbound model responses before returning to consuming applications; responses containing policy-violating content SHALL be blocked and replaced with a safe fallback response
- The AI Gateway SHALL maintain a versioned, centrally managed guardrail policy configuration; policy updates SHALL be applied consistently without requiring application-level changes
- The AI Gateway SHOULD support policy rule categories including: harmful and prohibited content, jailbreak and instruction-override patterns, PHI-sensitive topic steering, and domain-specific clinical safety guardrails for healthcare AI
- Where the guardrail policy rule set includes **clinical safety guardrail categories** (rules whose function is to determine whether an AI prompt or response poses a clinically safe or dangerous risk), those rules SHALL NOT be authored by the GOV function alone. Incorrect clinical safety rules represent a patient safety event in either direction — blocking a clinically appropriate AI response is a patient safety event; failing to catch a clinically dangerous AI output is also a patient safety event. A designated clinical subject matter expert (clinical informatics, medical affairs, or equivalent) SHALL be a required co-author and reviewer for every rule in the clinical safety category. The CAIO SHALL designate the clinical SME partnership arrangement and SHALL confirm it is in place before the AI Gateway processes any clinical decision support AI inference traffic
- The AI Gateway SHALL return a structured, non-descriptive rejection response when a prompt or response is blocked by guardrail policy; the response SHALL NOT disclose the specific rule that triggered the block
- The AI Gateway SHALL record guardrail policy outcomes — including policy rule category, action taken (block or allow), and a non-sensitive policy context identifier — in the AI Gateway audit log for every evaluated prompt and response
- The AI Gateway SHALL define and enforce a documented posture for streaming inference responses (server-sent events): either (a) the AI Gateway SHALL buffer the complete response stream before applying guardrail and DLP policy evaluation prior to delivery, or (b) the AI Gateway SHALL apply incremental evaluation with a defined minimum evaluation window, documented accuracy limitations, and the capability to terminate a stream mid-delivery on a policy violation; the streaming posture SHALL be specified in the AI Gateway policy configuration and SHALL NOT default to pass-through without evaluation

**Reference**: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-3 (Malicious Code Protection — adapted to AI content policy); SI-10 (Information Input Validation); SI-15 (Information Output Filtering); OWASP Top 10 for LLMs LLM01:2025 (Prompt Injection)

page_texts.21:
[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-2.9.07.md#principle-3-token-aware-and-cost-aware-rate-limiting]

#### Principle 3: Token-Aware and Cost-Aware Rate Limiting

**Description**: The AI Gateway SHALL enforce multi-dimensional rate limiting that accounts for token consumption, estimated compute cost, and request frequency — controls that are distinct from and additive to standard HTTP-layer rate limiting enforced by the enterprise API gateway. Token-aware rate limiting is the only effective enforcement point for cost exhaustion and AI-specific denial-of-service vectors.

**Rationale**: Token-based AI inference has a cost and resource profile fundamentally different from standard HTTP APIs. A single high-token prompt can consume the equivalent resource of thousands of standard API calls. Cost exhaustion, model extraction via high-volume probing, and adversarial compute drain cannot be adequately prevented by request-count-only rate limits applied at the HTTP layer. Token-aware controls at the AI Gateway are the only enforcement point that accounts for the economic and resource model of AI inference workloads.

**Capability Characteristics**:

- The AI Gateway SHALL enforce token-consumption rate limits per authenticated identity and per application context, with configurable thresholds for input token counts, output token counts, and total session token consumption
- The AI Gateway SHALL enforce cost-based rate limits expressed as estimated compute cost per identity per time period; cost thresholds SHALL be configurable per application criticality tier and SHALL generate alerts when approaching configured limits
- The AI Gateway SHALL enforce concurrent request limits per identity to prevent session flooding independent of token consumption
- Token and cost rate limits enforced by the AI Gateway SHALL be additive to and non-overlapping with standard HTTP request-rate limits enforced by the enterprise API gateway; the two components SHALL NOT share rate-limit counters or state
- The AI Gateway SHALL return a structured rate-limit response that includes a Retry-After indicator; for business-critical inference paths, the AI Gateway SHOULD implement request queuing rather than hard rejection for token-limit-triggered throttle events
- The AI Gateway SHALL log rate-limit events — including the limit dimension triggered, requesting identity, and current and threshold token or cost values — as security telemetry forwarded to the OPS monitoring function
- The AI Gateway SHOULD implement **output perturbation** — adding bounded noise or reducing output precision — as a complementary response when the rate-limit state store detects sustained query patterns consistent with model extraction attempts (systematic high-volume queries, broad coverage of the model's decision space, regular-interval probing). Output perturbation is applied in addition to hard throttling and serves to degrade the signal-to-noise ratio of extracted responses. The SBB SHALL document whether output perturbation is activated and the perturbation parameters applied, per [GUID-SEC-AI-APP-2.9.04 §Principle 5](GUID-SEC-AI-APP-2.9.04.md)

**Reference**: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-5 (Denial-of-Service Protection); AU-6 (Audit Record Review, Analysis, and Reporting); OWASP API Security API4:2023 (Unrestricted Resource Consumption); OWASP Top 10 for LLMs LLM04:2025 (Model Denial of Service)

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-2.9.07.md#principle-4-model-routing-and-provider-abstraction]

#### Principle 4: Model Routing and Provider Abstraction

**Description**: The AI Gateway SHALL route inference requests to model endpoints based on content classification, data sensitivity tier, capability requirements, and BAA coverage status — providing a stable, centralized routing layer that abstracts consuming applications from the underlying model topology and enforces provider selection rules that individual applications cannot override.

**Rationale**: Gainwell operates AI capabilities across internal model-serving infrastructure and multiple external AI providers with varying HIPAA compliance status and data handling agreements. Without a centralized routing layer, provider selection is implemented per application — inconsistently, without auditability, and without the ability to update routing policy centrally when provider agreements change. Application-level provider selection also cannot reliably prevent a configuration error from routing PHI to a provider without an active BAA. The AI Gateway is the only reliable enforcement point for provider governance and data residency requirements.

**Capability Characteristics**:

- The AI Gateway SHALL route all inference requests based on a centralized routing policy configuration; consuming applications SHALL specify capability requirements (model capability class, data sensitivity tier) and SHALL NOT directly specify model endpoint addresses or external provider API endpoints
- The AI Gateway SHALL enforce BAA routing rules: requests carrying a PHI or Regulated PII data sensitivity classification SHALL be directed only to model endpoints or external providers with an active, documented BAA; non-BAA routing for PHI-classified traffic SHALL be blocked and logged as a policy violation
- Data sensitivity tier assignments for application context identifiers SHALL be provisioned and managed by the GOV function; consuming applications SHALL NOT self-assert or override data sensitivity tier values; the AI Gateway SHALL NOT honor data sensitivity tier claims that are not present in the GOV-managed application context registry, and SHALL treat any request with an unrecognized context identifier as the highest applicable sensitivity tier pending formal classification
- The AI Gateway SHALL support routing policy dimensions including at minimum: data sensitivity tier (PHI, PII, non-sensitive), model capability class, application identity, and circuit-breaker state
- The AI Gateway SHALL provide transparent model endpoint abstraction: consuming applications SHALL invoke capability classes through a stable AI Gateway interface; changes to underlying model topology, provider failover, or model version updates SHALL be applied in routing policy without requiring application changes
- The AI Gateway SHALL log all routing decisions — including capability class requested, endpoint selected, BAA verification outcome, and any policy constraints applied — as part of the AI Gateway audit record
- The AI Gateway SHOULD implement circuit-breaker behavior for model endpoint and external provider routing, detecting sustained error rates or latency degradation and diverting traffic to fallback endpoints per configured policy
- All outbound connections from the AI Gateway to external AI provider endpoints SHALL enforce a minimum of **TLS 1.2**; **TLS 1.3 SHALL be used where the provider supports it**, consistent with [GUID-SEC-AI-APP-2.9.04 §Principle 6](GUID-SEC-AI-APP-2.9.04.md). Certificate validation SHALL be enforced on all external provider connections; connections to providers presenting self-signed, expired, or revoked certificates SHALL be rejected
- The AI Gateway's own outbound service credentials — API keys and tokens for external AI providers, credentials for the GOV policy feed, and credentials for the SIEM / audit log destination — SHALL be managed per [GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-2.9.03 §Principle 6](GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-2.9.03.md) and the enterprise secrets management standard (ADR-SEC-002). Cloud-native managed identities (AWS IAM roles for service accounts; Azure Managed Identity) SHALL be the preferred mechanism for any provider that supports them; static API keys are permitted only for providers that do not support managed identity and SHALL be stored in the enterprise-approved secrets manager with automated rotation enabled

**Reference**: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement); SC-7 (Boundary Protection); SC-28 (Protection of Information at Rest — data residency enforcement); IA-5 (Authenticator Management); HIPAA Security Rule §164.308(b)(1) (Business Associate Contracts and Other Arrangements)

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-2.9.07.md#principle-5-dlp-and-phi-control-at-the-ai-gateway-tier]

#### Principle 5: DLP and PHI Control at the AI Gateway Tier

**Description**: The AI Gateway SHALL perform Data Loss Prevention inspection on all prompts and responses, detecting and blocking PHI, PII, credential material, and other sensitive data categories before traffic crosses security or provider boundaries. DLP inspection at the AI Gateway tier is the authoritative, centralized enforcement point for data protection at the AI data plane.

**Rationale**: Application-layer DLP controls are application-specific and prone to inconsistent coverage across teams and products. The AI data plane is a high-risk channel for PHI exfiltration — enterprise users may include patient names, member IDs, clinical notes, or diagnosis codes in prompts, intentionally or inadvertently. Centralizing DLP at the AI Gateway ensures that every inference path is subject to the same DLP policy, independent of consuming application implementation. DLP at this tier also provides HIPAA compliance evidence that is independent of application-layer controls — critical when applications are developed by multiple teams or external parties.

**Capability Characteristics**:

- The AI Gateway SHALL apply DLP inspection to all inbound prompts prior to guardrail evaluation and model routing; prompts containing PHI, PII, credentials, or other sensitive data categories defined in the DLP policy SHALL be blocked or redacted based on the configured DLP policy action for that data category and routing context
- The AI Gateway SHALL apply DLP inspection to all outbound model responses prior to delivery to consuming applications; responses containing PHI or other sensitive data categories SHALL be blocked or redacted per DLP policy
- The AI Gateway's DLP policy SHALL be sourced from the centralized DLP rule set maintained by the GOV function; the AI Gateway SHALL NOT maintain independent DLP definitions without synchronization to the central policy source
- The AI Gateway SHALL log all DLP policy events — including data category matched, action taken (block or redact), requesting identity, routing destination, and a non-sensitive content context indicator — as security telemetry forwarded to OPS
- The AI Gateway SHALL NOT log full prompt or response content in standard operational logs; content containing PHI SHALL be routed only to HIPAA-compliant audit storage with appropriate access controls; standard audit log entries SHALL contain content hashes or anonymized context identifiers for correlation
- The AI Gateway SHALL NOT forward a prompt to a **non-BAA-covered endpoint** on the assumption that automated redaction has eliminated all PHI; automated DLP redaction has a known false-negative rate for free-text clinical and member content, and a prompt forwarded to a non-BAA-covered endpoint on the basis of redaction alone constitutes an unmitigated HIPAA risk; where redaction-as-routing-enabler patterns for non-BAA endpoints are operationally required, they SHALL be addressed in the paired RAD (GUID-SEC-AI-GW-RAD-3.9.07) with explicit documented risk acceptance approved by the CAIO and Privacy Officer
- Routing PHI-bearing traffic to a **BAA-covered internal model endpoint** is a governed, permitted use case under this principle and is not prohibited by the redaction restriction above; PHI-bearing prompts routed to BAA-covered internal endpoints SHALL still be subject to full DLP inspection and audit logging per this principle, but the DLP policy action for that routing context MAY be set to allow rather than block by GOV where the internal endpoint's BAA coverage and data handling controls warrant it

**Reference**: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement); MP-7 (Media Use); SI-12 (Information Management and Retention); HIPAA Security Rule §164.312(a)(2)(iv) (Encryption and Decryption); §164.312(e)(2)(ii) (Encryption of Data in Transit)

page_texts.24:
[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-2.9.07.md#principle-6-ai-specific-audit-evidence-generation]

#### Principle 6: AI-Specific Audit Evidence Generation

**Description**: The AI Gateway SHALL generate comprehensive, structured audit records for all AI inference traffic, capturing fields specific to AI operations and required for HIPAA compliance, security operations monitoring, and AI governance: token counts, model identifiers, routing decisions, guardrail policy outcomes, DLP disposition, cost estimates, and session metadata.

**Rationale**: Standard API gateway logs capture authentication events, HTTP status codes, and latency metrics — fields insufficient for HIPAA audit controls, security operations analysis, and AI governance compliance. AI-specific audit fields are required to demonstrate that guardrail policies were applied consistently, that PHI was handled in accordance with BAA routing rules, that token and cost controls operated as configured, and to support incident investigation involving AI systems. Without AI-specific audit evidence from a centralized enforcement point, compliance evidence is fragmented across application logs and cannot be reliably correlated with model-tier or provider-tier events.

**Capability Characteristics**:

- The AI Gateway SHALL generate a structured audit record for every processed inference request, including: timestamp, requesting identity, application context identifier, session or conversation identifier, data sensitivity tier, capability class requested, model endpoint or external provider selected, model version identifier, BAA routing rule applied, input token count, output token count, guardrail policy evaluation outcome (per category), DLP inspection outcome (per category), request latency, estimated cost, and a non-sensitive content context identifier for correlation
- The AI Gateway SHALL forward all AI Gateway audit records to the enterprise SIEM in real time or near-real time; audit record forwarding failures SHALL be treated as a security event requiring alerting
- Audit records SHALL be retained for a minimum of six years in compliance with HIPAA 45 CFR 164.530(j); retention management SHALL be the responsibility of the OPS function in coordination with the enterprise data retention policy
- The AI Gateway SHALL protect audit record integrity using append-only storage, cryptographic signing, or equivalent tamper-evident mechanisms; audit records SHALL NOT be modifiable or deletable by application-tier identities
- The AI Gateway SHALL NOT include full prompt or response content in audit records routed to standard SIEM or operational log pipelines; sensitive content SHALL be routed only to HIPAA-compliant audit storage with appropriate access controls and content-level encryption
- The AI Gateway SHOULD provide a queryable audit interface or export capability that allows the GOV function to retrieve audit evidence for compliance reporting and governance audits without requiring direct SIEM access

**Reference**: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-2 (Event Logging); AU-3 (Content of Audit Records); AU-9 (Protection of Audit Information); AU-12 (Audit Record Generation); HIPAA Security Rule §164.312(b) (Audit Controls); HIPAA 45 CFR 164.530(j) (Documentation Retention)

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-2.9.07.md#logical-component-patterns]

### Logical Component Patterns

The following patterns describe recurring AI Gateway security design scenarios. Each pattern is technology-agnostic — it describes the logical arrangement and sequencing of controls, independent of the specific AI gateway platform used. Illustrative platform-specific tooling is addressed in the paired Reference Architecture Detail ([GUID-SEC-AI-GW-RAD-3.9.07](ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-RAD-3.9.07.md)).

> **AI Gateway enforcement sequence**: For each inference request, the AI Gateway applies controls in the following normative order — (1) token and cost rate-limit check (Principle 3 / Pattern 2), (2) DLP inspection on the inbound prompt (Principle 5), (3) guardrail policy evaluation on the DLP-inspected prompt (Principle 2 / Pattern 1), (4) BAA routing verification and model dispatch (Principle 4 / Pattern 3), (5) guardrail policy evaluation on the model response, (6) DLP inspection on the response, (7) consumer response delivery with audit record written on completion. Implementations SHALL NOT evaluate guardrails before DLP on the inbound path.
page_texts.27:
[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-2.9.07.md#pattern-1-guardrail-policy-enforcement]

#### Pattern 1: Guardrail Policy Enforcement

**Context**: An enterprise application submits an LLM inference request containing natural language input from a user or automated process. Per the AI Gateway enforcement sequence, DLP inspection (Principle 5) has already been applied to the prompt. The AI Gateway now evaluates the DLP-inspected prompt against the active guardrail and content safety policy before forwarding to a model endpoint. If a policy violation is detected, the prompt must be blocked and a safe response returned.

**Pattern**:

1. The application forwards the inference request to the AI Gateway after enterprise API gateway authentication and handoff.
2. The AI Gateway retrieves the current guardrail policy configuration from its local policy cache (synchronized from the GOV policy feed).
3. The AI Gateway evaluates the prompt against configured policy categories: jailbreak and instruction-override patterns; prohibited and harmful content; PHI-sensitive topic steering rules; domain-specific clinical safety guardrails.
4. If a policy category match is detected, the AI Gateway blocks the prompt, records a guardrail violation event in the audit log (policy category, action, requesting identity — not the full prompt content), and returns a structured rejection response to the application.
5. If no policy violation is detected, the AI Gateway proceeds to BAA verification and model routing (Pattern 3 / Principle 4) and forwards the DLP-inspected, guardrail-cleared prompt to the selected model endpoint.
6. The returning model response traverses the same guardrail evaluation path before delivery to the application.

**Constraints**:

- Guardrail policy evaluation SHALL be applied to both inbound prompts and outbound responses.
- The rejection response SHALL NOT disclose which specific guardrail rule triggered the block.
- Policy cache refresh intervals SHALL be defined in the GOV policy configuration; stale policy caches SHALL generate an operational alert.

---
page_texts.28:
[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-2.9.07.md#pattern-2-token-budget-and-cost-control]

#### Pattern 2: Token Budget and Cost Control

**Context**: An enterprise application or user submits inference requests that may vary significantly in token consumption. The AI Gateway must enforce token and cost-based rate limits to prevent compute exhaustion, cost overrun, and model extraction via high-volume probing, without impeding legitimate use.

**Pattern**:

1. On receipt of each inference request, the AI Gateway identifies the requesting identity and application context from the pre-authenticated bearer token passed by the enterprise API gateway.
2. The AI Gateway retrieves current token and cost consumption counters for the requesting identity from its rate-limit state store.
3. The AI Gateway evaluates the projected input token count against configured per-session and per-period token limits for the identity tier and application criticality class.
4. If a limit would be exceeded, the AI Gateway returns a rate-limit response including a Retry-After value; for business-critical paths, it enqueues the request rather than rejecting it.
5. On successful inference completion, the AI Gateway records actual input and output token counts and updates consumption counters for the identity.
6. The AI Gateway calculates the estimated inference cost and compares it against the per-period cost cap for the identity; if a cost threshold is crossed, a telemetry alert event is forwarded to OPS.

**Constraints**:

- Token and cost counters SHALL be identity-scoped and SHALL NOT aggregate across identities.
- Token rate-limit state SHALL be maintained independently from the enterprise API gateway's HTTP request-rate limit state.
- Cost threshold alerts SHALL NOT block requests unless the configured cost cap for the period is exceeded.

---
page_texts.29:
[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-2.9.07.md#pattern-3-baa-governed-external-provider-routing]

#### Pattern 3: BAA-Governed External Provider Routing

**Context**: An inference request is destined for an external AI provider API — a capability not available on internal infrastructure. The AI Gateway must verify BAA routing requirements before forwarding the request outside the enterprise network boundary.

**Pattern**:

1. The AI Gateway receives a guardrail-cleared, DLP-inspected inference request with a routing context that resolves to an external provider capability class.
2. The AI Gateway evaluates the data sensitivity tier of the request (derived from application context identifier and DLP inspection outcome) against the BAA routing rule set from the GOV policy feed.
3. If the data sensitivity tier is PHI or Regulated PII, the AI Gateway verifies that the resolved external provider appears on the model's BAA-covered provider allowlist with an active agreement; if no active BAA entry is present, the request is blocked and a policy violation event is logged.
4. If the BAA routing check passes, the AI Gateway forwards the request to the external provider endpoint via a private network path (PrivateLink or equivalent private endpoint) using enforced TLS; requests SHALL NOT be forwarded to external provider public internet endpoints where private endpoint connectivity is available.
5. The AI Gateway logs the routing decision — external provider selected, BAA verification outcome, data sensitivity tier, and private endpoint indicator — as part of the audit record.
6. The provider response is returned to the AI Gateway, which applies response-path guardrail evaluation and DLP inspection before delivering to the application.

**Constraints**:

- PHI-classified traffic SHALL NOT be forwarded to any external provider without a verified, active BAA entry in the policy-managed allowlist.
- Private endpoint connectivity SHALL be the required path for BAA-governed external provider traffic where the provider supports it.
- BAA allowlist updates SHALL be applied via the GOV policy feed; out-of-band allowlist modifications SHALL be prohibited.

---
page_texts.30:
[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-2.9.07.md#pattern-4-ai-interaction-audit-trail]

#### Pattern 4: AI Interaction Audit Trail

**Context**: All inference requests processed by the AI Gateway must produce a complete, structured audit record satisfying HIPAA audit control requirements and supporting security operations monitoring and AI governance compliance reporting.

**Pattern**:

1. For each inference request, the AI Gateway opens an audit record at the point of receipt, recording: timestamp (ingress), requesting identity, application context identifier, session or conversation identifier, data sensitivity tier, capability class requested.
2. As the request progresses through enforcement stages, the AI Gateway appends outcomes to the audit record: guardrail policy evaluation results (per category, action taken); DLP inspection results (data categories matched, action taken); routing decision (endpoint or provider selected, BAA verification outcome); input token count.
3. On response receipt, the AI Gateway appends: output token count, response-path guardrail and DLP outcomes, estimated cost, total latency, and a non-sensitive content context identifier.
4. The completed audit record is written to the AI Gateway's append-only audit log and forwarded to the enterprise SIEM telemetry stream in real time.
5. Separately, if content-level detail is required for a HIPAA-compliant compliance investigation, a PHI-compliant audit record — with appropriate access controls and content-level encryption — is routed to the HIPAA audit log store managed by the OPS function.
6. Standard SIEM and operational log pipelines receive audit records with content hashes or anonymized identifiers only — no full prompt or response content.

**Constraints**:

- Every inference request SHALL produce an audit record regardless of whether it was blocked or forwarded.
- Audit record forwarding failures SHALL generate an alerting event; the AI Gateway SHALL buffer records locally until forwarding is restored.
- Full prompt and response content SHALL NOT appear in standard SIEM or operational log pipelines.

---

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-2.9.07.md#pattern-5-cloud-platform-topology]

#### Pattern 5: Cloud Platform Topology

**Context**: The AI Gateway must be logically positioned within an enterprise cloud service platform topology — AWS or Microsoft Azure — in a manner that satisfies the boundary protection, private connectivity, and traffic isolation requirements of this ABB. This pattern describes logical placement independent of specific product realization.

- Network-layer controls SHALL restrict AI Gateway inbound traffic to the enterprise API gateway enforcement point only; no direct routing path from application subnets to the AI Gateway SHALL be permitted.
- AI Gateway audit log data SHALL NOT traverse the public internet; forwarding SHALL use a private network path to the SIEM or logging infrastructure.

> **Cloud-specific network enforcement configuration** (Security Group rules, PrivateLink endpoint setup, VPC routing) is specified in the paired RAD: [GUID-SEC-AI-GW-RAD-3.9.07](ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-RAD-3.9.07.md).

    }

        Container(models, "Model Serving Endpoints", "Private Subnet", "Internal model endpoints; NSG permits inbound from AI Gateway subnet only")
    }

    System_Ext(ai_service, "External AI Service", "BAA-Governed Managed Service", "External model API (e.g., Azure OpenAI); connected exclusively via Private Endpoint in Platform Services VNet where provider supports it")
    System_Ext(siem, "Log Analytics / SIEM", "Observability Platform", "Audit record destination; AI Gateway forwards via Azure Monitor Private Link Scope (AMPLS) or hub-and-spoke log routing — log data SHALL NOT traverse the public internet")
    System_Ext(gov_feed, "GOV Policy Feed", "Internal VNet Routing", "Versioned signed policy bundles delivered to AI Gateway via internal VNet routing")

- The AI Gateway SHALL reside in a dedicated private subnet with no direct internet routing; all external AI service connectivity SHALL use private endpoint connectivity where the provider supports it.
- Network-layer controls SHALL restrict AI Gateway inbound traffic to the enterprise API management enforcement point only; no direct routing path from application subnets to the AI Gateway SHALL be permitted.
- AI Gateway audit log data SHALL NOT traverse the public internet; forwarding SHALL use a private network path to the SIEM or logging infrastructure.

> **Cloud-specific network enforcement configuration** (NSG rules, Private Endpoint setup, AMPLS configuration) is specified in the paired RAD: [GUID-SEC-AI-GW-RAD-3.9.07](ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-RAD-3.9.07.md).

**Constraints applicable to both cloud providers**:

- The AI Gateway SHOULD NOT share a subnet with the enterprise API gateway or model serving infrastructure; dedicated subnet isolation enables independent security group policy and facilitates blast-radius containment.
- Private endpoint connectivity SHALL be the required path for all BAA-governed external AI provider traffic.
- Network topology documentation SHALL be maintained and reviewed when provider connectivity options change.

## Architecture Decisions

The following key decisions were made during the design of this ABB. They are recorded to support future architects revisiting requirements under changed conditions.

| Decision ID | Decision | Rationale | Alternatives Rejected |
|---|---|---|---|
| ADR-GW-01 | AI Gateway deployed as a distinct logical component, not as an extension of the enterprise API gateway | AI-specific controls require an independent policy management lifecycle, audit stream, and operational footprint; co-location with the enterprise API gateway creates coupling that prevents independent policy updates, independent scaling, and isolated incident response | Extend enterprise API gateway with AI plugins — plugin controls share lifecycle with general API policy; commercially available AI gateway plugins do not provide the full required control surface |
| ADR-GW-02 | AI Gateway fails closed on unavailability | A fail-open gateway creates a bypass path that adversaries can deliberately induce via resource exhaustion; PHI reaching a model endpoint without DLP inspection or BAA routing verification is an unmitigated HIPAA risk regardless of the cause of unavailability | Fail-open with degraded-mode logging — the bypass window is unacceptable regardless of duration |
| ADR-GW-03 | DLP inspection is applied before guardrail evaluation on the inbound prompt path | If guardrail evaluation ran first, PHI in a blocked prompt could be written to guardrail event records before DLP has acted on it; DLP-first ensures PHI handling is determined before any downstream content inspection logging | Guardrail-first, DLP-second — rejected because of PHI exposure risk in guardrail event records |
| ADR-GW-04 | Data sensitivity tier is provisioned by GOV; consuming applications cannot self-assert | Self-asserted sensitivity classification is trivially bypassable; a misconfigured or adversarial application could route PHI to non-BAA endpoints by claiming a non-sensitive tier; GOV provisioning is the only model that provides an enforceable, auditable guarantee | Application self-assertion with GOV audit review — does not prevent PHI reaching an unintended endpoint before the error is detected |
| ADR-GW-05 | DLP redaction does not satisfy the BAA routing requirement for non-BAA-covered endpoints | DLP redaction has a known false-negative rate for free-text clinical content; treating a "redacted" prompt as categorically safe for non-BAA routing creates an unmanageable residual HIPAA risk | Permit non-BAA routing after DLP redaction as the default posture — rejected; available only as an explicit exception with documented CAIO and Privacy Officer approval per the paired RAD |
| ADR-GW-06 | Agentic AI and multi-turn orchestration patterns are explicitly deferred out of scope | Multi-turn tool-calling chains and agent-to-agent traffic have context accumulation characteristics that single-request guardrail and DLP evaluation cannot fully address; premature normative requirements risk creating false compliance assurance | Include agentic patterns with accuracy caveats — rejected in favor of a clean deferral to allow sufficient design time for controls effective for agentic traffic |

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-2.9.07.md#sbb-conformance-criteria]

### SBB Conformance Criteria

An SBB realizing this ABB SHALL satisfy the following minimum conformance criteria. These criteria are intended to be verifiable through testing, architecture review, and operational evidence.

| Control | Principle | Minimum Conformance Criterion | Recommended Testing Approach |
|---|---|---|---|
| Distinct enforcement plane | 1 | No network path exists from application subnets to model serving endpoints or external AI provider APIs that bypasses the AI Gateway | Network topology review; attempt direct model API call from application subnet — SHALL be blocked at network layer |
| Fail-closed on gateway unavailability | 1 | When the AI Gateway process is stopped or fails, inference requests receive a 5xx response; no traffic reaches model endpoints | Chaos test: stop AI Gateway; verify model endpoint receives zero traffic; verify 503 response to applications |
| Partial pipeline degradation fail-closed | 1 | When the guardrail evaluation service is unavailable while the AI Gateway is healthy, all inference requests are blocked — not passed through | Chaos test: remove guardrail service dependency; submit inference request — SHALL receive 503, not a model response |
| Guardrail policy enforcement | 2 | Known jailbreak prompts from an agreed test corpus are blocked with a structured rejection response that does not disclose the specific rule triggered | Automated test: submit benchmark jailbreak corpus; verify 0% pass rate; verify rule identity is not disclosed in the response body |
| Streaming posture enforcement | 2 | The configured streaming posture (buffered or incremental with a documented minimum evaluation window) is applied; pass-through streaming without evaluation is not present | Code review of AI Gateway streaming configuration; integration test confirming evaluation occurs before or during stream delivery |
| Token and cost rate-limit enforcement | 3 | Requests exceeding the configured token limit for a test identity are throttled with a Retry-After indicator; a separate identity's counters are unaffected | Load test: exceed configured token limit for identity A; verify throttle response for A; verify identity B request succeeds |
| BAA routing enforcement | 4 | PHI-classified requests targeting a non-BAA-covered endpoint are blocked; PHI-classified requests targeting a BAA-covered endpoint succeed | Integration test: PHI-classified request to non-BAA destination — SHALL be blocked; to BAA-covered destination — SHALL succeed |
| DLP inspection on inbound prompts | 5 | Prompts containing known synthetic PHI patterns are detected and blocked or redacted per the configured DLP policy action | DLP test suite: submit prompts with synthetic PHI (names, MRNs, diagnosis codes); verify block or redact action per policy |
| Audit record completeness | 6 | Every inference request — blocked and forwarded — produces a structured audit record containing all required fields defined in Principle 6 | Schema validation test; verify 100% audit record rate including blocked requests; validate all required fields present |
| Audit record PHI exclusion | 6 | Full prompt and response content does not appear in SIEM-bound audit records; only content hashes and context identifiers are present | Submit request containing synthetic PHI; inspect SIEM-bound record; verify PHI content absent and content hash present |
| Audit record tamper evidence | 6 | Audit records are stored in an append-only, tamper-evident store; application-tier service accounts cannot modify or delete records | Access control review: verify application service accounts lack write and delete permissions on the audit log store |
